extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers; authors and people interested in literary life and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and practical observations about speaking, writing, reputation-management, publicity, and performance drawn from a 19th-century literary essay. Includes advice for authors, actors in private theatricals, and general conduct in literary society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversation to shape and model writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Spoken language is plastic and shapes thought; rough out thoughts in talk as an artist models in clay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘It shapes our thoughts for us;—the waves of conversation roll them as the surf rolls the pebbles on the shore.’’ Spoken language lets you 'pat and coax, and spread and shave, and rub out, and fill up, and stick on' easily; talking 'roughs out' ideas that are later turned into more finished written work. Metaphor: writing/printing is like shooting with a rifle (you may hit or miss); talking is like playing at a mark with the pipe of an engine (if within reach and time, you will hit). Use conversation deliberately to refine and form your ideas before committing them to print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-finalizing catch-phrases that shut down debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain final expressions ('Fust-rate', 'prime', 'a prime article', 'That tells the whole story') are terminal and socially stigmatizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These expressions are 'final' and 'blast the lineage' of the speaker; they are used by vulgar and conceited people and by well-meaning folk who imitate them. Phrases intended to stop discussion rarely tell 'the whole story' and should be avoided because they close off nuance and debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategically 'jockey' your books and public presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should manage publicity judiciously: reveal works sparingly, time exposure, and use promotion tactically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include: 'letting the public see your animal just enough, and not too much; holding him up hard when the market is too full of him; letting him out at just the right buying intervals; always gently feeling his mouth.' Keep multiple books 'spinning' by reviving them with advertisement, puffs, or quotations. Be aware that frequent extracts in papers often signal an upcoming new book or edition—'the extracts are ground-bait.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not needlessly attack or 'break' conventional reputations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a tacit social compact in literary communities to avoid disturbing popular reputations of established celebrities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include respect for age, wealth, good-nature, or managerial risk (a favorite of the pit). Newspapers and critical notices often support these reputations with pleasant phrases. The writer advises restraint: 'Don’t steal their chips; don’t puncture their swimming-bladders; don’t come down on their pasteboard boxes; don’t break the ends of their brittle and unstable reputations.' Wantonly attacking such reputations is presented as a social and professional mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust the instant feeling that a freshly written line is already 'old' or seen before
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly formed lines or ideas often feel 'a hundred years old' immediately after composition; this sensation should not be trusted as evidence of prior copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains a theory: new formulas have roots in long trains of thought and are 'virtually old' when they appear. He therefore distrusts sudden convictions of antiquity and does not allow them to bully him out of original thoughts. He also muses that the apparent rapid 'ageing' of ideas scales with their importance (a great calamity seems ancient almost at once).

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor natural, unexaggerated acting in private theatricals
rubrics_metrics.description: Private theatricals are best served by genuine, unrouged, unspoiled performers who avoid stagey mouthing, ranting, and striding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer prefers seeing 'real gentlemen and ladies, who do not think it necessary to mouth, and rant, and stride,' and values a 'fresh, unrouged, unspoiled, high bred young maiden' with a pleasant voice and lithe figure. He contrasts country lyceum-hall performances with gilded metropolitan salons, implying different expectations, but consistently favors naturalism over exaggerated stage mannerisms in private amateur productions.
